Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage describes robustness as stable model performance or behavior under changes in prompts, inputs, task conditions, environments, or evaluation setup. Many papers apply this broad framing to prompt paraphrases and ordering, noisy or degraded inputs, distribution shifts, adversarial perturbations, new opponents or environments, and other superficial or challenging variations, often contrasting robustness with brittleness to minor changes. Smaller lines of work define it more narrowly as retaining pre-learned general capabilities after task-specific fine-tuning, or as worst-case performance on rare shifted inputs rather than average performance. Another recurring minority usage applies the term to the persistence of an artifact rather than the model, for example a jailbreak prompt, backdoor, or watermark remaining effective or detectable after defenses, fine-tuning, editing, or paraphrasing.

Space of facets. Papers most often organize robustness by the source of variation: prompt and instruction changes, input noise or superficial perturbations, out-of-distribution data, adversarial or jailbreak attacks, and deployment across opponents, seeds, or environments. A smaller strand explicitly separates out-of-distribution from adversarial robustness, and some benchmark papers place robustness inside broader Trustworthiness framings or alongside Safety and Consistency. Across linked constructs, robustness is frequently discussed alongside Generalization, while Selection bias is used to describe one recurring failure mode. The same label is also used for distinct objects, model stability, retention after adaptation, and persistence of watermarks or backdoors.

Space of measurement. Papers link robustness to 45 measurement instruments and 16 behavioral indicators. The most common instruments are AdvBench, GSM-Hard, MMBench, MMLU-Redux, and SVAMP, plus 40 other instruments; these are mostly benchmarks or dynamic environments that probe performance under adversarial inputs, out-of-domain tests, shuffled answer choices, text perturbations, varying task parameters or seeds, and degraded context, and one paper also uses a judge-based comparison. Among behavioral indicators, links cluster around attack, generation, and agent behaviors. These operationalizations usually match the dominant definition by scoring stability under perturbation or shift, though some operationalize robustness as retention of earlier capabilities after fine-tuning or as watermark and backdoor persistence under attack or overwriting.

Links. Across linked constructs, several papers claim causal relationships from Generalization to Robustness, and one paper claims the reverse from Robustness to Generalization. Several papers also claim causal relationships from Reasoning and from In-context learning to Robustness, and one paper separately claims a causal relationship from Out-of-distribution generalization to Robustness and from Robustness to Out-of-distribution generalization. Papers also relate robustness to Generalization non-causally, and one paper reports that robustness correlates with Selection bias.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage describes robustness as stable model performance or behavior under changes in prompts, inputs, task conditions, environments, or evaluation setup. Many papers apply this broad framing to prompt paraphrases and ordering, noisy or degraded inputs, distribution shifts, adversarial perturbations, new opponents or environments, and other superficial or challenging variations, often contrasting robustness with brittleness to minor changes. Smaller lines of work define it more narrowly as retaining pre-learned general capabilities after task-specific fine-tuning, or as worst-case performance on rare shifted inputs rather than average performance. Another recurring minority usage applies the term to the persistence of an artifact rather than the model, for example a jailbreak prompt, backdoor, or watermark remaining effective or detectable after defenses, fine-tuning, editing, or paraphrasing.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Papers most often organize robustness by the source of variation: prompt and instruction changes, input noise or superficial perturbations, out-of-distribution data, adversarial or jailbreak attacks, and deployment across opponents, seeds, or environments. A smaller strand explicitly separates out-of-distribution from adversarial robustness, and some benchmark papers place robustness inside broader Trustworthiness framings or alongside Safety and Consistency. Across linked constructs, robustness is frequently discussed alongside Generalization, while Selection bias is used to describe one recurring failure mode. The same label is also used for distinct objects, model stability, retention after adaptation, and persistence of watermarks or backdoors.

characterization_sections.label: Space of measurement.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link robustness to 45 measurement instruments and 16 behavioral indicators. The most common instruments are AdvBench, GSM-Hard, MMBench, MMLU-Redux, and SVAMP, plus 40 other instruments; these are mostly benchmarks or dynamic environments that probe performance under adversarial inputs, out-of-domain tests, shuffled answer choices, text perturbations, varying task parameters or seeds, and degraded context, and one paper also uses a judge-based comparison. Among behavioral indicators, links cluster around attack, generation, and agent behaviors. These operationalizations usually match the dominant definition by scoring stability under perturbation or shift, though some operationalize robustness as retention of earlier capabilities after fine-tuning or as watermark and backdoor persistence under attack or overwriting.

characterization_sections.label: Links.
characterization_sections.text: Across linked constructs, several papers claim causal relationships from Generalization to Robustness, and one paper claims the reverse from Robustness to Generalization. Several papers also claim causal relationships from Reasoning and from In-context learning to Robustness, and one paper separately claims a causal relationship from Out-of-distribution generalization to Robustness and from Robustness to Out-of-distribution generalization. Papers also relate robustness to Generalization non-causally, and one paper reports that robustness correlates with Selection bias.

definition_agreement.reason: Most papers use robustness for the same broad phenomenon: a model or agent maintaining intended performance, reasoning, behavior, or safety when prompts, inputs, environments, data distributions, or other operating conditions are perturbed, shifted, or made more challenging. A few papers instead apply the term to the persistence of things like watermarks, backdoors, jailbreak prompts, or evaluation methods, so the literature is not a strict consensus, but the dominant uses are complementary facets of stability under stress rather than outright contradictions.
